questions.question: Sarah wants to spend a day in nature looking for wildlife. She doesn't have a car, so she needs to travel by train. She has a limited budget and is not interested in shopping.

questions.question: What is Maya's main priority for the near future?

questions.question:
Read this email from your English-speaking friend Alex and the notes you have made.

***
From: Alex
Subject: Your new course!

Hi,

How are you? I heard you started a new course last week. What kind of course is it? [Tell Alex]

I'd love to know if you are enjoying it. Is the teacher nice? [Great!]

Maybe I can join you next time. When is the next class? [Answer]

Let's meet up this weekend to talk about it. Which day is better for you? [Suggest]

Write back soon,
Alex
***

Write your email to Alex using all the notes. You should write about 100 words.
questions.explanation: To get a high score in B1 Writing Part 1, make sure you answer all four notes clearly: 1) Tell Alex what kind of course it is (e.g., photography, cooking, Italian). 2) Confirm that you are enjoying it and that the teacher is great. 3) State when the next class is. 4) Suggest a specific day (Saturday or Sunday) to meet up. Keep your tone friendly and informal, and aim for around 100 words.

questions.question:
Choose one of the following tasks (article or story). Write about 100 words.

Option 1: Article
You see this notice on an international English website for young people:

*Articles wanted!*
LEARNING SOMETHING NEW
What is a new skill you would like to learn? Why do you want to learn it? Is it easy or difficult for young people to learn new things?
Write an article answering these questions.

OR

Option 2: Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story. Your story must begin with this sentence:

*It was my first day at the class.*
Write your story.
questions.explanation: For Option 1 (Article), give your article an interesting title, use paragraphs to organize your ideas, and express your opinion clearly. For Option 2 (Story), make sure you start with the exact sentence provided, use narrative tenses (Past Simple, Past Continuous) to describe what happened, and create a clear beginning, middle, and end. Aim for about 100 words.

questions.question:

questions.question:
A group of friends has a free Saturday afternoon together in town. Talk together about the different things they could do, and decide which would be the best option.

questions.explanation: In Part 3, you interact with your partner. Make suggestions, ask for your partner's opinion, agree or disagree politely, and try to reach a decision together by the end of the 2-3 minutes.

questions.question:

passages.title: New Library Services
passages.text: Hello everyone. I am here to tell you about the exciting changes coming to our local library next month. First, we are introducing a new online reservation system. You will be able to book books from home using your library card number. We are also opening a new study area on the second floor, which will be equipped with ten high-speed computers. For those who enjoy reading outside, we are launching a 'Books in the Park' scheme where you can borrow items from a mobile stand near the fountain. Please note that the library will be closed for renovations on the 15th of July. If you need help with your digital skills, we are starting free weekly workshops every Wednesday morning. Finally, if you have any suggestions, please leave a note in the suggestion box located next to the main entrance.

passages.title: School Trip to France
passages.text: Hello everyone. I am here to give you the final details about our upcoming school trip to France. We will be departing from the school gates at 7:30 am on Monday morning, so please make sure you arrive on time. We are staying at a lovely hotel in the countryside, which is famous for its large swimming pool. On the first day, we will visit a local museum to learn about history. The most exciting part of the trip will be the visit to the chocolate factory on Wednesday, where we can taste everything! For lunch, we will have a picnic in the park, but please remember to bring a bottle of water. Finally, don't forget to bring your camera to take photos of the beautiful scenery. I am sure we will have a fantastic time!

passages.title: New Sports Centre Opening
passages.text: Hello everyone! I am delighted to announce that the Riverside Sports Centre will finally open its doors to the public next Monday. We have spent months preparing the facilities. If you are interested in swimming, our main pool is 25 metres long and has a special area for children. For those who prefer fitness, the gym is equipped with the latest machines, and we offer a variety of classes including yoga and aerobics. We are currently looking for a receptionist to join our team, so please check our website if you are interested. Membership fees are very reasonable, and if you sign up before the end of the month, you will receive a discount of 15 percent on your first year. We also have a cafe on the ground floor where you can relax after your workout. We look forward to seeing you there!

passages.title: Interview with a Game Designer
passages.text: Interviewer: Today we are talking to Sarah Jenkins, who designs video games for a living. Sarah, was it always your dream to work in this industry? Sarah: Actually, no. I studied architecture at university. I loved drawing buildings, but I found the work a bit slow. One day, a friend showed me how to code a simple game, and I was hooked. I realized that game design is like architecture, but you can build entire worlds that people can interact with. Interviewer: That sounds fascinating. What is the most challenging part of your job? Sarah: People think it is just playing games all day, but it is actually very stressful. We have strict deadlines. If the game isn't ready for the holiday season, the company loses a lot of money. Sometimes I spend 12 hours a day staring at code. Interviewer: Do you ever get tired of it? Sarah: Sometimes, but then I see someone playing a game I helped create, and their face lights up. That feeling is worth all the hard work. Interviewer: What advice would you give to young people wanting to enter the field? Sarah: Don't just play games—learn how they are made. Start with simple tools and don't be afraid to make mistakes. Your first game will probably be terrible, and that is perfectly fine!

passages.title: Interview with Travel Blogger Sarah Jenkins
passages.text: Interviewer: Sarah, you've been blogging for five years now. What made you start? Sarah: I was working in an office and felt bored. I took a trip to Peru and realized I wanted to share my experiences. Interviewer: Was it hard to get started? Sarah: Yes, I didn't know anything about photography or writing for an audience. I had to learn everything from scratch. Interviewer: Many people think travel blogging is just a holiday. What do you say to them? Sarah: It's definitely not! I spend hours editing photos and researching locations. It's a full-time job. Interviewer: Do you ever get lonely? Sarah: Sometimes, but I meet so many interesting people on the road that it balances out. Interviewer: What is your favorite part of the job? Sarah: Seeing a place I've only read about in books. It's magical. Interviewer: Any advice for beginners? Sarah: Be yourself. Don't try to copy other bloggers. Authenticity is what people want to see.

passages.title: Interview with a young chef
passages.text: Interviewer: Today we are joined by Maya, a 22-year-old chef who recently opened her first restaurant. Maya, was it always your dream to cook professionally? Maya: Honestly, no. I studied graphic design first! But I spent all my free time helping my grandmother in her kitchen. I realized that the pressure of a busy service was actually where I felt most alive. Interviewer: Many people find the long hours in a kitchen difficult. How do you manage? Maya: It is exhausting, I won't lie. You are on your feet for twelve hours. But I have a great team, and we support each other. If I didn't love the creativity of inventing new dishes, I would have quit months ago. Interviewer: What is the most challenging part of your job? Maya: People think it's the cooking, but it's actually the management. Ordering ingredients, dealing with staff, and keeping the budget in check—that's the real work. The cooking is the reward at the end of the day. Interviewer: Do you have advice for young people wanting to enter the industry? Maya: Don't expect to be a head chef immediately. Start at the bottom, learn how to clean, how to prep, and be humble. You need to be willing to fail a few times before you get it right.

passages.title: Interview with a young chef
passages.text: Interviewer: Today we are talking to Sarah Jenkins, who recently opened her own restaurant at just twenty-two. Sarah, was it always your dream to be a chef? Sarah: Actually, no. I wanted to be a musician, but I loved cooking for friends. Then, I took a summer job in a kitchen and realized I preferred the heat of the stove to the stage! Interviewer: Was it difficult to start your own business so young? Sarah: The hardest part wasn't the cooking, but the paperwork. I spent weeks talking to banks and finding the right location. I almost gave up once, but my mentor encouraged me to keep going. Interviewer: What is the most popular dish on your menu? Sarah: Definitely the spicy vegetable stew. I thought people would find it too hot, but they love it. I use a secret spice mix from my grandmother. Interviewer: What do you do when you are not working? Sarah: I try to get away from food entirely! I go hiking or read books. If I stay in the kitchen too long, I lose my creativity. Interviewer: What advice would you give to other young people? Sarah: Don't be afraid to make mistakes. Every burnt meal is a lesson.

passages.title: A New Beginning
passages.text:
Moving to a new city is often described as an exciting adventure, but for me, it felt more like a challenge I wasn't ready for. Last summer, my parents announced that we were moving from our quiet village to the bustling city of Manchester. I had lived in the same house for fourteen years, and the thought of leaving my friends and my favourite local park was devastating.

When we first arrived, the noise was the biggest shock. Unlike the peaceful nights I was used to, the city never seemed to sleep. There were sirens, traffic, and people talking at all hours. For the first two weeks, I barely left my room. I felt like an outsider looking in, convinced that I would never fit into this fast-paced environment. I spent most of my time messaging my old friends, feeling sorry for myself.

However, everything changed when I joined a local photography club. I had always enjoyed taking pictures, and I thought it might be a good way to get out of the house. On my first day, I met a girl named Sarah who was also new to the area. We started exploring the city together, looking for interesting buildings and street art to photograph. Through her eyes, I began to see the city differently. Instead of just seeing traffic and noise, I started to notice the beautiful architecture and the vibrant culture.

It has been six months now, and I can honestly say I don't regret the move. While I still miss my old friends, I have built a new life here. I have learned that moving isn't just about changing your address; it is about changing your perspective. You have to be willing to step outside your comfort zone to find the hidden gems in any new place. If you are facing a big move, my advice is to find a hobby or a group that shares your interests. It makes the world feel a lot smaller and much friendlier.

passages.title: A Life-Changing Summer in Peru
passages.text: Last summer, I decided to do something completely different. Instead of spending my holidays at home, I signed up for a volunteer program in a small village in the Peruvian Andes. I had always wanted to travel, but I wanted to do more than just visit tourist sites; I wanted to make a real difference. When I arrived, I was surprised by how different everything was. The air was thin, the mountains were breathtaking, and the local community was incredibly welcoming. My main job was to help build a new classroom for the primary school. I had never held a hammer or painted a wall before, but the local builders were very patient with me. They taught me how to mix cement and how to work as part of a team. It was hard physical work, especially in the heat, but I felt a great sense of achievement every evening. In the afternoons, I helped the children with their English homework. They were so eager to learn, and we often spent hours laughing as we tried to communicate through gestures and simple words. Living without electricity and limited internet access was a challenge at first. I missed my friends and the comforts of home, but as the weeks passed, I realized that I didn't need those things to be happy. I learned to appreciate the simple things, like a shared meal or a beautiful sunset over the peaks. This experience changed my perspective on life. I realized that we don't need much to be happy, and that helping others is one of the most rewarding things you can do. I returned home with a new sense of purpose and a promise to myself that I would continue volunteering in the future. I have already started looking for local opportunities in my own city.

passages.title: Rising Star: An Interview with Leo Vance
passages.text:
At just sixteen, Leo Vance has already made a name for himself in the world of competitive swimming. We caught up with him at his local training centre in Manchester. 'I started swimming when I was five,' Leo explains, drying off after a two-hour morning session. 'My parents took me to the pool every weekend, but I didn't really take it seriously until I joined a club at ten.'

Leo’s routine is demanding. He wakes up at 4:30 a.m. to be in the water by 5:15 a.m. 'It’s tough, especially in winter when it's dark and cold outside,' he admits. 'But when you’re in the pool, you forget the time. You just focus on your strokes.' Despite the hard work, Leo insists he has a normal social life. 'People think athletes don't have time for friends, but I make sure I see my mates on Friday nights. It’s important to switch off.'

His biggest challenge so far was the National Youth Championships last year. 'I was so nervous before the final race,' he recalls. 'I almost pulled out, but my coach reminded me why I started. I ended up winning silver.' That medal changed his perspective. 'It wasn't just about the prize; it was about proving to myself that I could handle the pressure.'

Looking ahead, Leo has his sights set on the international stage. 'The dream is the Olympics, obviously. But for now, I’m focused on improving my technique. My coach says I’m strong, but my turns need work.' When asked if he has any advice for other young athletes, he is humble. 'Don't let the sport define who you are. Enjoy it, work hard, but remember to have fun. If you stop enjoying it, you’ll never reach your potential.'

passages.text:
Hello everyone, and welcome to our school trip to the Science Museum. Before we go inside, I have some important information for you, so please listen carefully and write down these details on your worksheets.

First, we are very lucky because there is a special exhibition on at the moment. It is called 'Robots', and it shows how machines have changed over the last hundred years. This exhibition has been very popular, and it is actually ending next month, on the twelfth of October, so make sure you don't miss it today.

Now, a little bit of history. The museum is quite old. It was first opened to the public in 1925, and it has grown a lot since then.

There are many amazing things to see, but the most popular object in the whole museum is a large model of a spaceship. You can find it in the transport gallery on the second floor.

After your tour, you might want to visit the museum shop. They have some great souvenirs. You can get books and keyrings, but the shop is currently offering a discount on posters, which are very cheap today.

Finally, about our travel arrangements. We need to meet back at the main entrance at four o'clock. The bus back to school will leave at 4.30 exactly. Please do not be late, as the driver cannot wait. Enjoy your visit!

passages.title: Interview with a Travel Blogger
passages.text:
Interviewer: Today I'm talking to Elena Rossi, a successful travel blogger. Elena, welcome. Why did you first start your blog, 'Elena's Footsteps'?

Elena: Well, I didn't plan to make it my job! I actually started it when I went on a gap year to South America. My parents were really worried, so I promised to write regular updates so they'd know I was safe. I didn't think anyone else would read it, but then other travelers started finding my posts and asking for advice.

Interviewer: That's amazing. You've been to so many countries. Which one stands out the most?

Elena: People always ask this! I love Japan for its food, and Iceland for the landscapes, but my absolute favorite was Albania. I didn't know much about it before going, but the local people were incredibly welcoming. One family even invited me into their home for dinner when I got lost. That kindness is what I remember most.

Interviewer: Traveling isn't always easy, though. How do you deal with things when they go wrong?

Elena: Oh, I've had missed flights, lost luggage, and food poisoning! At first, I used to get really stressed and angry. But I quickly realized that doesn't help. Now, I just accept that problems are part of the adventure. I try to stay calm and look for a solution, often by asking locals. They are usually happy to help a confused tourist.

Interviewer: You usually travel by yourself. Do you prefer that?

Elena: I do. When you travel with friends, you tend to stay in your own little bubble. But when you're on your own, you're forced to talk to strangers, which means you make new friends much faster. Of course, it can be lonely occasionally, but the freedom to decide where to go next without arguing is worth it.

Interviewer: What's the most challenging part of being a professional blogger?

Elena: People think it's a permanent holiday, but it's hard work. The toughest thing for me is the lack of a routine. I'm constantly moving, which makes it hard to exercise regularly or eat healthily. I don't mind the long hours spent editing photos or writing posts, because I love doing that, but not having a proper home base can be exhausting.

Interviewer: Finally, what tips do you have for someone wanting to start a travel blog?

Elena: Don't just write about the famous tourist spots that everyone knows. Try to find a unique angle. Write about your personal feelings and the small details, like the smell of a local market. And most importantly, write because you love it, not because you want to get free hotel rooms. Readers can tell if you aren't being genuine.

Interviewer: Thank you, Elena!

passages.title: Great Day Trips in the Region
passages.text:
A. Highwood House
Step back in time at this stunning 18th-century manor. Explore the beautifully landscaped gardens and take a guided tour of the historic rooms. Tickets are quite pricey, and because of its remote countryside location, there is no public transport, so you will need to drive.

B. The Reedlands
This peaceful nature Reserve is a paradise for bird watchers and wildlife lovers. Take a relaxing boat trip along the river for a very low price. The Reserve is located right next to a train station, making it easy to reach. There is a small cafe on board, though there are no shops here.

C. Peak Heights
For those who love being active, a trip up the mountain is a must. Enjoy challenging hiking trails or take the cable car to the summit for breathtaking views. There is an excellent souvenir shop and a cafe at the top. It is expensive and only accessible by car.

D. Seabreeze Cove
Spend a relaxing day at this beautiful coastal village. Walk along the sandy beach, taste fresh local seafood at the harbor restaurants, and browse the small local art galleries. A regular bus service runs from the city center, and it is very budget-friendly.

E. Deep Stone Caves
Discover amazing rock formations on a fascinating guided underground tour of these ancient caves. It is cool inside, so bring a jacket! A Bus stop is located just outside the entrance. There is a great gift shop selling unique local stone crafts. Booking in advance is recommended.

F. Greenwood Park
Get your adrenaline pumping with a tree-top canopy walk and adventure sports in this deep forest. It is a fantastic day out for active people, though entry fees are high. You will need a car to get here, and remember to bring your own food as there are only picnic areas and no shops.

G. Oakhaven Town
This beautiful historic town is famous for its weekly market, where you can buy unique local crafts and gifts. Learn about the town's past on a free walking tour. It is very cheap to visit and has a direct train link to the city center.

H. The Cosmos Centre
An interactive science and space museum perfect for a rainy day. Explore the planetarium and hands-on exhibits. Located in the city center, it is easily reached by bus or train. It has a great gift shop and cafe, though tickets are expensive.

passages.title: An Interview with Maya Lin
passages.text:
We talked to sixteen-year-old runner Maya Lin about her life on and off the track. Maya recently won the national junior 800-metre championship, but she remains surprisingly down-to-earth.

Interviewer: Maya, congratulations on your gold medal! How did you first get into running?
Maya: Thanks! Actually, it was by accident. When I was eleven, my school's running team was short of one person for a relay race. The coach saw me running to catch the school bus and asked me to fill in. I didn't even have proper running shoes! I ended up running really fast, and the coach suggested I join the club. Before that, I preferred playing video games and reading. I never imagined I would become an athlete.

Interviewer: How do you manage to balance your training with your schoolwork?
Maya: It isn't easy. I train for about two hours every day after school, and more on weekends. I have to be very organized. I do my homework on the bus or during lunch breaks. My friends are very understanding, though they sometimes complain that I can't hang out with them on Friday nights because I have to sleep early for Saturday morning practice. But they always come to support me at my races, which means a lot.

Interviewer: Do you ever feel too much pressure before a big race?
Maya: Definitely. Before a race, my hands shake and I feel sick. But my coach taught me to view that nervous energy as a positive thing. She says it shows my body is preparing to run fast. Once the race starts, all the worry disappears and I just focus on my breathing and my steps. I don't think about winning; I just try to beat my own personal best time.

Interviewer: What are your goals for the future?
Maya: Of course, the Olympics is the ultimate dream, but that is a long way off. For now, I want to focus on my next race and keep improving. I also want to finish my school exams with good grades because education is important to me. If I have one piece of advice for other young people, it's to try new things. You might discover a talent you never knew you had!
